subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Coffee in Mecca and Cairo
description: A short lesson to help you apply Coffee in Mecca and Cairo.

hook.text: By 1510, coffee had reached Mecca and Cairo. Both cities erupted with coffeehouses almost overnight.

buildup.text: Cairo's coffeehouses lined the streets near Al-Azhar University—scholars and students were regulars.

discovery.text: Mecca's coffeehouses doubled as news hubs. Pilgrims returned home carrying coffee beans and brewing knowledge.

twist.text: The governor of Mecca banned coffee in 1511, citing disorder. The Cairo sultan overruled him within weeks.

climax.text: Coffee was too popular, too profitable, and too embedded in religious life to suppress.

punchline.text: Banning coffee in Mecca lasted weeks. Demand won.

quiz.question: Who overruled the Mecca coffee ban of 1511?

details.summary: By the early 1500s, coffeehouses were thriving in Mecca and Cairo. They became social hubs for scholars, merchants, and travelers. Religious authorities debated whether coffee was permissible, sometimes banning and then reinstating it. The debates could not overcome coffee's unstoppable popularity.
details.whyItMatters: Mecca and Cairo were where coffee evolved from a devotional aid into a social beverage. Their coffeehouses set the template adopted by the Ottoman Empire and then Europe.
takeaways: Coffeehouses thrived in Mecca and Cairo by the early 1500s
Religious authorities repeatedly debated coffee's permissibility
These cities established the coffeehouse as a social institution

faq.question: Why was coffee banned in Mecca in 1511?
faq.answer: The governor of Mecca convened a council of physicians and jurists who declared coffee an intoxicant and banned it. However, the Sultan of Cairo overruled the ban, noting that coffee was widely consumed in Egypt without issue. The episode showed coffee's popularity was politically unstoppable.

faq.question: What role did Cairo play in coffee's spread?
faq.answer: Cairo was a major commercial hub connecting Africa, Asia, and Europe. Its bustling coffeehouses attracted international merchants who carried the coffee habit to Constantinople and eventually to European trading cities. Cairo was coffee's gateway to the wider world.
